paragraphs: A network's ability to memorize arbitrary data does not by itself explain what it learns during ordinary training. This paper investigates memorization alongside model capacity, generalization, and adversarial robustness. Its results suggest that deep networks tend to learn simple patterns before memorizing noise, making the course of training relevant to understanding their behavior.

The experiments identify qualitative differences between gradient-based training on real data and on noise. They also examine explicit regularization, including dropout. With appropriate tuning, regularization can make networks fit noise datasets less successfully without harming their ability to generalize on real data. The qualification about tuning matters: the finding concerns suitably chosen regularization.

Together, these observations suggest that memorization depends partly on the training data itself. The authors therefore question whether dataset-independent notions of effective capacity can explain generalization under gradient-based training. The contribution is evidence for an explanation that accounts for both what a network can represent and how learning unfolds on particular data.
icml-2017-a-closer-look-at-memorization-.tldr: Experiments suggest that deep networks learn simple patterns first and that memorization depends on the data and training process.

paragraphs: Newton-ADMM aims to accelerate conic optimization, a framework for solving a broad class of convex problems. Its starting point is an existing iterative method, ADMM. Instead of only following that method's successive updates, the authors express the differences between consecutive iterates as equations whose solution represents a fixed point of the iteration.

They then use a nonsmooth Newton method to solve those equations, applying the approach to the Splitting Cone Solver, or SCS. By extending the theory of semismooth operators, they establish quadratic convergence to a solution. This describes a rapid rate of error reduction in the convergence analysis; the empirical comparison separately addresses actual solver speed.

On a number of tested problems, Newton-ADMM is significantly faster than SCS. It also requires essentially no parameter tuning and can produce certificates that a primal or dual problem is infeasible when appropriate. The method can be specialized for particular convex problems, giving the fixed-point approach relevance beyond a single generic solver implementation.
icml-2017-a-semismooth-newton-method-for.tldr: Newton-ADMM accelerates conic optimization by applying a nonsmooth Newton method to equations derived from ADMM updates.

paragraphs: This paper presents REBEL, a boosting method for classification problems with multiple classes. The motivating goal is a simple, inspectable learning system that is accurate while requiring little data and training time. Alongside the boosting framework, the authors introduce a family of weak learners called localized similarities, which supply the components used by the method.

The theoretical result concerns fitting the training data: the framework is proved to minimize training error at an exponential rate for any dataset. That is a claim about how quickly training error is reduced. It is distinct from the question of whether the resulting classifier will perform well on examples outside the training set.

The authors investigate that second question empirically using synthetic and real datasets. They report a consistent tendency to avoid overfitting and evaluate REBEL against state-of-the-art methods on MNIST and standard UCI datasets. The stated findings support its practical effectiveness, while keeping the observed resistance to overfitting separate from the formal guarantee about training error.
icml-2017-a-simple-multi-class-boosting-.tldr: REBEL combines multiclass boosting with localized-similarity weak learners, offering an exponential training-error guarantee and encouraging empirical generalization.

paragraphs: Many questions about a discrete distribution concern its overall structure rather than the names assigned to its outcomes. Examples include its support size, support coverage, entropy, and proximity to uniformity. These are symmetric properties. Earlier work had developed separate estimators and analytical tools to estimate each of these quantities with asymptotically optimal sample requirements.

The paper shows that one estimator, profile maximum likelihood, can provide a common approach. It is a plug-in estimator: a distribution estimate serves as the basis for estimating the desired property. The key contribution is that the same estimation principle comes with sample-competitiveness guarantees across all symmetric properties, rather than requiring a different principle for each one.

For the four properties explicitly listed, the result is stronger: profile maximum likelihood achieves asymptotically optimal sample efficiency. This concerns how much sampled data estimation requires in the asymptotic regime. The significance is a unified statistical foundation for problems that previously had separate sample-optimal treatments, with the broader competitiveness claim distinguished from optimality for the named properties.
icml-2017-a-unified-maximum-likelihood-a.tldr: Profile maximum likelihood provides one sample-competitive estimator for symmetric distribution properties and asymptotically optimal estimates for several prominent examples.

paragraphs: A softmax operator combines values in a way that lies between selecting the largest and taking an average. In sequential decision making, this can help favor high-value choices while avoiding complete commitment to a single option. The paper examines the commonly used Boltzmann softmax operator and shows that it can exhibit problematic behavior.

The authors study an alternative differentiable operator with a non-expansion property. In plain terms, applying it does not enlarge differences between value inputs. This mathematical feature supports convergent behavior in learning and planning, connecting the choice of value-combination rule to the stability of the larger decision-making procedure.

They also introduce a variant of SARSA that uses the new operator. The resulting algorithm computes a Boltzmann policy whose temperature varies by state, allowing the policy's degree of concentration to depend on the situation. The paper establishes convergence for this algorithm and reports favorable practical performance. Its contribution combines an operator-level property with a concrete learning algorithm built around that property.
icml-2017-an-alternative-softmax-operato.tldr: A differentiable, non-expanding softmax operator supports a convergent SARSA variant with state-dependent Boltzmann temperatures.

paragraphs: Low-rank approximation represents a large matrix through a smaller structure that retains important information. It is useful for reducing noise and identifying signals in data. This paper introduces Spectrum-Revealing LU, or SRLU, a truncated LU factorization designed for this purpose, together with a fast algorithm for computing it.

The authors derive error bounds for both the matrix approximation and its singular values. Their analysis suggests that SRLU is competitive with leading deterministic and randomized low-rank methods in computational cost and approximation quality. This gives theoretical support for using an LU-based construction as an effective approach to low-rank approximation.

Numerical experiments show that SRLU preserves sparsity, exposes important features and variables, and supports efficient updates. They also find approximation accuracy close to the best possible. These observations address several practical needs together: maintaining sparse structure, retaining useful information, and revising an approximation efficiently. The authors describe it, to their knowledge, as the first practical LU variant to deliver effective and efficient low-rank approximation.
icml-2017-an-efficient-sparsity-preservi.tldr: SRLU uses a truncated LU factorization for accurate, efficiently updatable low-rank approximations that preserve sparsity in experiments.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning can be unstable, with variability in learning reducing performance. Averaged-DQN addresses this problem through a simple modification to DQN: it averages previously learned estimates of Q-values. These estimates describe the values of actions, so variation in them can affect the targets used to train the learning system.

The proposed averaging reduces the variance of approximation errors in those target values. The intended effect is a steadier training signal and, consequently, a more stable learning procedure. To explain the mechanism, the authors examine sources of value-estimation error and develop an analytical comparison within a simplified model.

Experiments on the Arcade Learning Environment show significantly improved stability and performance from the extension. The analysis and experiments serve different roles: the simplified model helps explain why averaging can help, while the benchmark demonstrates its effect in the tested setting. The contribution is a small change to the value-estimation procedure with both analytical motivation and empirical evidence of improved learning.
icml-2017-averaged-dqn-variance-reductio.tldr: Averaged-DQN averages earlier Q-value estimates to reduce target-error variance and improve learning stability and benchmark performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to find anomalous patterns occupying a connected portion of a graph. Such a task arises in network intrusion detection, community detection, surveillance, and disease-outbreak detection. Connectivity matters because the target is a related group of nodes, but searching directly over connected subgraphs creates a difficult combinatorial optimization problem.

The authors replace that search with a convex relaxation that incorporates connectivity and conductance constraints on candidate subgraphs. This gives a principled optimization formulation for the desired graph structure. They then develop an efficient solver based on mirror descent for the relaxed problem, connecting the structural model to a computational method.

The paper establishes convergence guarantees for the algorithm and evaluates feasibility and performance on real networks and very large simulated networks. The guarantees concern solving the relaxation, while the experiments examine its usefulness for detection at scale. Together, the contributions address both how to express connected-pattern detection mathematically and how to make the resulting optimization practical on large graph data.
icml-2017-connected-subgraph-detection-w.tldr: A convex relaxation and mirror-descent solver make connected anomalous-subgraph detection computationally tractable, with convergence guarantees and large-network experiments.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning tasks can be easier to specify when desired rewards and behavioral constraints are stated separately. This is particularly relevant when physical systems interact with people and safety constraints matter. Constrained Policy Optimization, or CPO, brings such constraints into policy search for neural-network controllers operating in high-dimensional settings.

CPO provides guarantees of near-satisfaction of constraints at each training iteration. The emphasis on the whole training process matters because behavior during learning can be consequential, as well as the behavior of the final policy. Near-satisfaction is the stated guarantee; it should not be read as exact constraint satisfaction at every step.

The theoretical foundation is a bound connecting the expected returns of two policies to an average measure of divergence between them. This links changes in policy behavior to changes in expected outcomes. Experiments on simulated robot locomotion tasks demonstrate the approach with safety-motivated constraints. The paper thus combines a policy-search algorithm, a supporting theoretical result, and evidence from constrained control tasks.
icml-2017-constrained-policy-optimizatio.tldr: CPO trains neural-network policies with guarantees of near-constraint satisfaction throughout training and demonstrations on simulated robot locomotion.

paragraphs: Deep Voice is presented as a production-quality text-to-speech system whose components are all deep neural networks. It includes models for phoneme segmentation, text-to-phoneme conversion, phoneme duration, fundamental frequency, and audio synthesis. Replacing each component with a neural model reduces reliance on the extensive feature engineering and domain expertise associated with traditional systems.

Two technical contributions address segmentation and sound generation. The segmentation model detects phoneme boundaries using connectionist temporal classification loss. For audio synthesis, the system uses a WaveNet variant with fewer parameters and faster training than the original. These changes support a neural speech pipeline spanning linguistic processing through waveform generation.

The authors demonstrate inference faster than real time and describe optimized WaveNet inference kernels for both CPUs and GPUs. Those kernels achieve speedups of up to 400 times over existing implementations. The upper-bound wording matters: it is the reported maximum speedup. The system establishes groundwork for fully end-to-end neural speech synthesis while demonstrating a practical pipeline built entirely from neural components.
icml-2017-deep-voice-real-time-neural-te.tldr: Deep Voice builds every text-to-speech component with neural networks and demonstrates faster-than-real-time synthesis with optimized inference.

paragraphs: The paper addresses two related matrix problems: finding the top k generalized eigenvectors and finding the top k vectors in canonical-correlation analysis. It introduces LazyEV and LazyCCA for these respective tasks. Their running times scale linearly with the size of the input and with the number k of requested vectors.

The algorithms also improve how running time depends on two spectral quantities, the matrix condition number and the eigengap. The authors call this double acceleration because both dependencies have a square-root form. They present this combination as the first such result for either of the two problems, extending the efficiency improvement beyond input-size scaling alone.

A further contribution removes dependence on the eigengap from alternative guarantees. These gap-free results instead use an accuracy parameter, epsilon, with a running-time dependence of 1/sqrt(epsilon). This offers an accuracy-based way to state computational requirements. Overall, the paper provides related algorithms whose guarantees address input size, the number of desired directions, and the spectral or accuracy quantities governing the computation.
icml-2017-doubly-accelerated-methods-for.tldr: LazyEV and LazyCCA offer linear input-size scaling, double acceleration in spectral parameters, and gap-free accuracy-dependent guarantees.

paragraphs: Principal component regression is commonly associated with finding leading principal components before performing regression. This paper gives an approximation algorithm that avoids explicitly constructing those components. Instead, it reduces the task to repeated calls to a ridge-regression solver, treating that solver as a reusable computational building block.

For multiplicative accuracy 1+gamma, the algorithm requires roughly gamma to the power of minus one ridge-regression calls, with logarithmic factors suppressed. The previous result required roughly gamma to the power of minus two calls under the same notation. The improvement therefore concerns how the number of solver calls grows as the requested accuracy becomes tighter.

The authors obtain the reduction through two approximation tools: a stable recurrence for matrix Chebyshev polynomials and a degree-optimal polynomial approximation to the matrix sign function. Avoiding explicit principal-component construction makes the approach suitable for large-scale PCR instances. The polynomial techniques also have potential independent value, especially for designing iterative methods, although that broader usefulness is presented as a possibility.
icml-2017-faster-principal-component-reg.tldr: A stable polynomial construction reduces approximate principal component regression to fewer ridge-regression calls without explicitly computing principal components.

paragraphs: Online top-eigenvector learning presents a tradeoff between computational efficiency and regret. Matrix multiplicative weight updates achieve optimal regret, but computing matrix exponentials makes them slow. Follow-the-perturbed-leader methods are faster, yet their regret is worse by a factor of sqrt(d) for matrices of dimension d.

The proposed follow-the-compressed-leader framework combines the desirable aspects of these approaches. It matches the optimal regret of matrix multiplicative weight updates up to polylogarithmic factors, while running no slower than follow-the-perturbed-leader. The qualification about logarithmic factors is part of the result: the regret is nearly optimal rather than stated as an exact match.

The central idea is to compress the matrix multiplicative weight strategy into a very small dimension: three in the adversarial setting and one in the stochastic setting. These are dimensions of the compressed strategy, not restrictions on the original input matrices. The resulting framework resolves the stated open question of obtaining both computational efficiency and nearly optimal regret for online eigenvector learning.
icml-2017-follow-the-compressed-leader-f.tldr: Compressing matrix multiplicative weight updates yields online eigenvector learning with nearly optimal regret and the speed of faster perturbed-leader methods.

paragraphs: Successful-looking GAN training does not necessarily mean that the generated distribution is close to the target distribution. This paper shows that the two distributions may remain far apart under standard metrics even when training appears successful. It therefore separates success in the training game from generalization measured by broader distributional comparisons.

The authors also establish a positive result: generalization does occur under a weaker measure called neural net distance. A second theoretical result concerns equilibrium in the generator-discriminator game. For a Wasserstein training objective, an approximate pure equilibrium exists when generator capacity and training-set sizes are moderate. The statement is an existence result under the specified setting.

That equilibrium result motivates MIX+GAN, a protocol that can be combined with existing GAN training methods. Experiments show improvements for some of those methods. The paper consequently offers both a warning about how GAN success is interpreted and constructive results: a metric supporting generalization, an equilibrium guarantee, and a training protocol inspired by the theory.
icml-2017-generalization-and-equilibrium.tldr: GANs can generalize under neural net distance while failing standard metrics, and an equilibrium result motivates the empirically useful MIX+GAN protocol.

paragraphs: Input convex neural networks are scalar-output networks whose parameters are constrained so that the output is convex in some or all of the inputs. The architecture can still be deep. Its defining feature concerns the shape of the output as selected inputs vary, creating a structure that can be used during inference.

Given some inputs, the remaining inputs can be inferred by optimization. The paper develops methods for this inference process, for optimization, and for learning, while also analyzing what the networks can represent. It shows that many existing architectures can be made input-convex through a minor modification and introduces specialized optimization algorithms for the resulting setting.

Applications include structured prediction, missing-data completion, and reinforcement learning. Experiments cover multi-label prediction, image completion, and reinforcement learning, with improvements over the existing state of the art in many cases. The contribution is a way to combine neural representations with convex optimization over inputs, supported by architectural analysis, tailored algorithms, and evidence across several task types.
icml-2017-input-convex-neural-networks-5.tldr: Input convex neural networks constrain their parameters to support efficient inference by convex optimization over selected inputs.

paragraphs: Algebraic and logical expressions can have the same meaning despite looking very different. This paper introduces neural equivalence networks to learn continuous representations that capture such semantic equivalence. The goal is to connect symbolic expressions with neural representations while preserving information about what those expressions mean.

The central difficulty is that representations must follow an expression's syntax because meaning is built compositionally from its parts. Yet a small syntactic change can produce a large change in meaning. Continuous neural architectures must therefore account for both equivalent expressions with very different structures and expressions whose similar structures conceal substantial semantic differences.

The authors evaluate the architecture on equivalence checking across a highly diverse collection of algebraic and Boolean expression types. They report that it significantly outperforms existing architectures in this evaluation. The finding supports the proposed network as a step toward combining symbolic and continuous reasoning, with the demonstrated task specifically being recognition of equivalence across the tested expression families.
icml-2017-learning-continuous-semantic-r.tldr: Neural equivalence networks learn continuous representations of symbolic meaning and improve equivalence checking across diverse algebraic and Boolean expressions.

paragraphs: Predicting deterioration in hospitalized patients requires interpreting both physiological measurements and the circumstances in which they were collected. This paper models clinicians' decisions about when to take vital signs or order laboratory tests as informative. The timing of observations becomes part of a continuous-time model for prognosis, alongside the measured values themselves.

A marked Hawkes process represents observation timing, with its intensity controlled by unobserved clinical states. A switching multitask Gaussian process models the physiological observations. An absorbing semi-Markov process represents the hidden clinical states and captures informative censoring, so the way a patient episode ends is also included in the model.

The parameters are learned from previously recorded electronic health record episodes using an EM-based algorithm. Evaluation uses a cohort admitted to a major medical center over three years. The authors report significantly better risk prognosis than deployed medical risk scores and other baseline machine-learning algorithms. The findings support jointly modeling patient physiology, observation timing, and episode termination in that evaluated cohort.
icml-2017-learning-from-clinical-judgmen.tldr: A continuous-time patient model uses physiology, clinicians' observation timing, and informative episode endings to improve risk prognosis in a hospital cohort.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization is valued for making effective use of limited evaluations, but its focus on global optimization makes higher-dimensional problems difficult. This paper adapts that sample-efficient approach to a local search. It restricts optimization of the acquisition function, which guides the next evaluations, to the neighborhood of a Gaussian search distribution.

The search distribution moves toward regions with high objective values. Its update uses an information-theoretic approach with a Bayesian interpretation: the distribution expresses prior knowledge about where the optimum lies, and each iteration weights that knowledge by the likelihood that a location is optimal. This connects local stochastic search to probabilistic reasoning about promising locations.

The authors demonstrate the algorithm on benchmark objective functions and a continuous robotic task. In the robotic example, imitation learning supplies an informative prior. The approach therefore offers a way to use prior knowledge and sample-efficient evaluation within a moving local search region, with empirical evidence supporting its effectiveness on the tested optimization and motor-skill problems.
icml-2017-local-bayesian-optimization-of.tldr: Local Bayesian optimization searches near an adaptively updated Gaussian distribution to bring sample-efficient optimization to higher-dimensional motor-skill problems.

paragraphs: Policy sketches describe a task as a sequence of named subtasks without explaining how to perform them. This paper uses such sketches to guide multitask reinforcement learning. The supplied structure identifies relationships between tasks, while leaving the agent to learn behavior without intermediate rewards, subtask-completion signals, or the other detailed guidance described in the abstract.

Each named subtask is associated with a modular subpolicy. Tasks that use the same subtask share that module's parameters, allowing behavior to be learned jointly across tasks. A decoupled actor-critic objective supports this shared learning even when the tasks have dissimilar reward functions, while optimizing rewards for complete task policies.

Evaluation spans three environments with discrete and continuous control and sparse rewards available only after multiple high-level subgoals. Sketch-guided learning performs better than existing task-specific or shared-policy techniques in these experiments. It also produces interpretable primitive behaviors that can be recombined for rapid adaptation to new tasks, giving the learned modules value beyond the original task combinations.
icml-2017-modular-multitask-reinforcemen.tldr: High-level policy sketches guide shared subpolicy learning, improving sparse-reward multitask performance and enabling rapid recombination for new tasks.

paragraphs: Natasha addresses optimization of a nonconvex function expressed as an average of n smooth functions. The paper develops stochastic first-order methods for finding approximate stationary points, where the gradient is small. Their performance depends on a parameter sigma associated with the smallest negative Hessian eigenvalue, which measures how strongly nonconvex the objective is.

This parameter plays a role analogous to strong convexity in convex optimization. Accounting for it allows the authors to obtain theoretical improvements over known results for a range of sigma values. The methods can also be used to find approximate local minima. The claimed speed advantage is qualified as theoretical and applies within the stated parameter range.

The analysis reveals a threshold separating two regimes among the currently fastest methods. Above that threshold, their dependence on the number of component functions scales as n to the two-thirds power; below it, the scaling is n to the three-quarters power. This highlights how the degree of nonconvexity can change which algorithmic behavior gives the strongest available guarantee.
icml-2017-natasha-faster-non-convex-stoc.tldr: Natasha obtains theoretical optimization improvements in certain regimes by making algorithmic performance depend on the objective's degree of nonconvexity.

paragraphs: Experimental design asks which candidate measurements or design points to select when only a limited number can be used. This paper considers selecting k points from n candidates, each with dimension p, so that a chosen optimality criterion is approximately satisfied. The aim is to make this selection computationally tractable while preserving a strong approximation guarantee.

The proposed algorithm finds a design within a factor of 1+epsilon of optimal when k grows linearly with p. Existing results required k to grow superlinearly with p. The improvement therefore concerns the relationship between the number of selected points and their dimension, reducing the selection size needed for the stated guarantee.

The algorithm also supports all popular optimality criteria, whereas earlier methods handled only one or two. This broadens the range of design objectives covered by one approach. Numerical evaluations on synthetic and real-world design problems support its practical effectiveness. The contribution combines a stronger selection-size guarantee with broader criterion coverage and empirical evidence on design problems.
icml-2017-near-optimal-design-of-experim.tldr: A tractable experimental-design algorithm achieves near-optimal selection with a number of points linear in dimension across popular optimality criteria.

paragraphs: OptNet places optimization problems inside neural networks as trainable layers. Specifically, each such layer solves a quadratic program, allowing it to express constraints and dependencies among hidden states that conventional convolutional or fully connected layers often struggle to capture. The surrounding network remains trainable end to end.

The paper explains how sensitivity analysis, bilevel optimization, and implicit differentiation provide exact derivatives through these layers and with respect to their parameters. It also introduces a solver using GPU-based batch computations within a primal-dual interior-point method. The solver supplies backpropagation gradients at virtually no extra cost beyond solving the optimization problem itself.

Applications demonstrate how this architecture can learn constrained behavior. In a highlighted example, it learns to play 4-by-4 mini-Sudoku from input and output games without being given the rules beforehand. The example supports the authors' claim that the architecture can learn hard constraints better than other neural architectures. The contribution joins an expressive layer design with differentiation techniques and an efficient implementation.
icml-2017-optnet-differentiable-optimiza.tldr: OptNet makes quadratic programs differentiable neural-network layers, enabling end-to-end learning of constraints and structured dependencies.

paragraphs: Many machine-learning objectives are sums of individual functions. First-order optimization methods use gradients, while second-order methods also use Hessians to describe curvature. Because curvature can reduce the number of iterations needed in principle, second-order information offers a possible route to more efficient optimization of these finite-sum problems.

Although full Hessian computations can be expensive in high dimensions, individual component Hessians may be much easier to compute or manipulate, for example when they have low-rank structure. The paper asks whether this apparent computational opportunity translates into better guarantees. It provides evidence that second-order information does not improve efficiency in the worst-case sense considered.

The negative conclusion is explicitly about worst-case guarantees, so it does not establish that curvature information is never useful. The authors also discuss additional assumptions and algorithmic approaches that might circumvent the result. The contribution clarifies a boundary between the promise of fewer iterations and guaranteed overall efficiency, while identifying the possibility of stronger results under further structure or different approaches.
icml-2017-oracle-complexity-of-second-or.tldr: The paper gives worst-case evidence against an efficiency advantage from second-order information in finite-sum optimization while discussing possible ways around the result.

paragraphs: This paper studies the performance cost of differential privacy in online linear optimization. It considers both full-information feedback and bandit feedback, where the learner has more limited observations. Performance is measured by regret over T rounds, and the proposed private algorithms achieve the optimal square-root dependence on T.

In the full-information setting, the regret bound is O(sqrt(T) + 1/epsilon), where epsilon is the privacy parameter. Privacy contributes an additive term rather than multiplying the term that grows with time. This is the sense in which the authors say privacy may be obtained for free: the leading time-dependent rate remains unchanged, while the bound still includes a privacy-dependent cost.

For bandit linear optimization, the bound is O(sqrt(T)/epsilon), so privacy scales the time-dependent term. This improves the previously best known bound of O(T^(2/3)/epsilon). The result also covers non-stochastic multi-armed bandits as a special case. Together, the bounds distinguish how privacy affects learning under rich feedback versus limited feedback.
icml-2017-the-price-of-differential-priv.tldr: Private online linear optimization achieves square-root regret in time, with additive privacy cost under full information and multiplicative cost under bandit feedback.

paragraphs: Wasserstein GAN, or WGAN, is introduced as an alternative approach to training generative adversarial networks. The paper connects the behavior of the training process to the choice of distance between probability distributions. Its theoretical work examines those connections and establishes the soundness of the corresponding optimization problem.

The authors show that the approach can improve training stability and eliminate problems such as mode collapse. They also report meaningful learning curves, making the training signal useful for debugging and choosing hyperparameters. These are related practical benefits: a more interpretable account of training progress can help users assess and adjust the learning process.

The paper's significance lies in bringing mathematical foundations and training behavior together. The distribution-distance analysis explains the motivation for a different optimization formulation, while the stated findings describe improvements it can deliver in practice. The claims describe capabilities of the proposed approach; they do not establish that every possible WGAN training run must be stable or free of collapse.
icml-2017-wasserstein-generative-adversa.tldr: WGAN connects GAN training to distribution distances to improve stability, address mode collapse, and provide useful learning curves.
